transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-03-30
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Location: Zoom (recording available)
Attendees: Samira Patel (Redwood AE), Miguel Reyes (Redwood SE), Aisha Khan (Novus CTO), Markus Lee (Platform Eng), Ellen Park (Security), Jonas Meyer (ML Infra)

Summary (auto):
- Deep dive on on-prem/air-gapped artifact delivery, offline licensing activation, and GPU driver requirements.
- Discussed runtime performance trade-offs (KV cache, batching, quantization) and recommended warmup/bench approaches.
- Agreed next steps: share artifact tarball checksums, offline licensing checklist, and schedule bench run in Novus staging.

Transcript:
[00:00] Samira: hey everyone thanks for carving out time. Quick roll call?
[00:06] Aisha: Aisha here, CTO at Novus. Markus here as well, same room.
[00:09] Markus: yep Markus, platform. Ellen on security. Jonas on infra.
[00:13] Samira: awesome. Miguel, want to kick us off with a quick overview of the on-prem package and what's in the artifact?
[00:20] Miguel: sure, thanks. so the artifact we hand off for air-gapped installs is basically a signed tarball that contains the runtime binaries, model runtime container images as flat tar files, a driver compatibility manifest, and an offline license bundle. there's also a signed checklist and sha256sums for every piece.
[00:36] Miguel: typical contents: redwood-runtime.tar.gz, images/ redwood-models-<ver>.tar, drivers/ nvidia-driver-535.xx.rpm (we list supported drivers), and license/offline-license-<customer>.lic which is an encrypted token you install with our installer.
[00:52] Ellen: quick question, when you say encrypted token is that bound to hardware or to a VM id? how does revocation work?
[00:57] Miguel: good question. license tokens are issued per-cluster id. for air-gapped we have an offline activation flow: you generate a cluster id locally, send the fingerprint via an approved channel (sftp or physical usb) to Redwood licensing team, they return a signed license blob that you install. revocation is handled server-side in our control plane but for private/offline you get an administrative revocation manifest we include in the next patch bundle.
[01:19] Ellen: ok so initial activation requires a one-time outbound or physical transfer, then updates are signed and included in subsequent bundles. is that right?
[01:25] Miguel: exactly. and we can support pure sneakernet where you slip a usb into a secured transfer appliance. we also support an air-gapped SFTP appliance if you want a more automated flow.
[01:33] Aisha: what about the GPU drivers? we run RHEL 8.6 across nodes and we're currently on kernel 4.18. we also have some existing NCCL and CUDA deps.
[01:41] Miguel: kernel 4.18 is pretty old for newer CUDA stacks; our recommendation for optimal perf with the runtime is NVIDIA driver 535+ and CUDA 12.x. that typically needs 5.x kernels. we do have compatibility matrices in the driver manifest. if you can't upgrade kernel, we can lean on specific older driver artifacts but you'll probably sacrifice some perf/throughput.
[02:00] Jonas: can you be specific on perf numbers? our SLO is p95 generation latency < 150ms for the 2k context case on the staging cluster (we have A100-ish nodes).
[02:09] Miguel: yes. quick note, numbers vary by model and quantization. for example we ran internal bench on a 70B model, q4_k_m quant, on an A100 80GB with our runtime and saw steady-state token throughput ~420 tokens/sec with p50 token latency ~6ms and p95 token latency ~25ms for short sequences. end-to-end generation latency for a 512-token response depends on batching and prefix cache: with warm KV-cache and small batch sizes we saw p95 ~130-160ms in our lab, so you're in range but need warm-up and KV cache priming.
[02:45] Markus: you said warm KV-cache — what's the memory footprint and how long to fill?
[02:49] Miguel: KV cache is per-request KV memory; for long-context models it can be large. typical numbers: for a 70B model, KV cache per token is about 1.2MB (approx — depends on head/kv dtype), so at 2k context that's ~2.4GB per request. with moderate batching we keep multiple contexts in GPU memory; we recommend a KV capacity plan. priming depends on your workload—if you have a set of repeated prompts, cache hits happen immediately after the first request; for cold starts we advise a short warmup run (a few hundred tokens per model) to populate shared prefix caches for common routes.
[03:18] Ellen: that sounds big. what's the recommended approach on air-gapped to avoid OOMs?
[03:22] Miguel: there are a few levers: quantization (int8 or q4 variants) reduces KV memory and model size; dynamic batching policies that bound concurrent in-flight contexts; and configuring our cache eviction policy—LRU with size caps per GPU. we can also enable streaming so large responses are produced with smaller working sets.
[03:38] Aisha: about quantization, do you support post-training quantization or do you ship quantized model variants?
[03:43] Miguel: we provide pre-quantized variants in the artifact bundle for the most common profiles (q4_k_m, int8 where applicable). we also provide the quantization recipes and a local offline tool that can re-quantize if you need a custom profile, but that tool has kernel-level dependencies and must be run on a machine with host-level CUDA.
[03:58] Jonas: will the quantization tool be included in the offline tarball?
[04:01] Miguel: yes, we include the binary and documentation. note though that re-quantizing large models offline can take hours and needs scratch storage; we include sha256s to verify outputs.
[04:10] Ellen: on compliance: we need audit logs proving the offline licensing handshake happened and who installed what. does the installer generate a tamper-evident audit log?
[04:17] Miguel: installer creates an audit bundle: signed install log with timestamps, merkle hash of installed artifacts, and the license fingerprint. we can also optionally ship an HSM-bound signing step if you have an onboard HSM.
[04:28] Ellen: great. please include sample logs with redaction guidance.
[04:31] Samira: noted. Miguel, can you walk through the offline license activation flow step-by-step?
[04:36] Miguel: sure. step 1: run redwood-cluster-init which outputs cluster-id.json and a signed fingerprint. step 2: transfer the fingerprint file to Redwood via the approved carrier (sftp appliance or physical usb) to licensing@redwood.io (we provide PGP and an SFTP enclave). step 3: Redwood validates the fingerprint, produces signed license blob offline and returns license-<id>.lic. step 4: you run redwood-license-install --file license-<id>.lic; installer validates signature and writes a local license manifest into /var/lib/redwood/license.json. step 5: runtime checks license manifest on boot; periodic license refresh is optional and done via next patch bundle.
[05:09] Markus: is there a heartbeat required to Redwood? we can't have any egress from production.
[05:13] Miguel: no persistent heartbeat required. the normal hosted setup uses heartbeats, but air-gapped mode is offline-first. only initial activation and optional refresh require out-of-band transfer.
[05:24] Aisha: let's talk about patches. how do we receive security patches for the runtime in a timely fashion?
[05:29] Miguel: patches are delivered as patch bundles signed by Redwood. we provide a patch manifest and delta tarballs so you can apply smaller updates. for critical security fixes we can do an expedited offline transfer via SFTP enclave or physical courier depending on your policy.
[05:41] Jonas: performance tuning: what runtime knobs are most important for our use case?
[05:44] Miguel: top three: batch size ceilings (controls latency vs throughput), prefetching and KV cache warmup policy (controls p95 after cold starts), and quantization profile. also kernel driver tuning — setting CUDA persistence mode, disabling preemption in kernel where supported, and ensuring NVLINK topology is optimal for multi-GPU.
[05:59] Jonas: NVLINK topology — do you have recommendations for multi-GPU interconnects?
[06:02] Miguel: yes, for heavy cross-GPU KV sharing we recommend fully connected NVLINK meshes or DGX-style topologies. if your hardware is a mix, we configure model sharding / tensor parallelism accordingly in the runtime to minimize cross-node traf.
[06:15] Aisha: can we get a simple runbook for benchmarking? we want to reproduce your numbers.
[06:19] Miguel: absolutely. steps we'll share: a) load the artifact bundle and verify sha256s; b) install drivers in our manifest order (driver -> cuda toolkit -> nccl), reboot nodes; c) load model images via offline docker load; d) run warmup traffic with our bench-runner for 10 minutes across expected prompt shapes; e) capture p50/p95 token latency and tokens/sec. we'll include suggested bench configs for your A100 nodes.
[06:43] Ellen: any gotchas with kernel/driver combos and RHEL?
[06:46] Miguel: yes, older RHEL kernels sometimes require a specific driver build flag. we include an rpm and a prebuilt module for common kernels. if your kernel is custom, we'll provide a DKMS package and build instructions in the offline bundle.
[06:58] Markus: about image signing and verification — we have strict supply-chain controls. how do you sign the images and can we perform verification locally?
[07:05] Miguel: images are signed with cosign and we provide the public key in the bundle. the installer verifies container image signatures and file checksums before importing images to the local registry. we include the cosign binary and verification script.
[07:17] Aisha: great. can you explain the quantization tradeoffs quickly — int8 vs q4_k_m — for our finance workload where hallucination risk is sensitive?
[07:25] Miguel: int8 tends to be faster and smaller but can introduce slightly higher numeric drift in downstream logits; q4_k_m is a 4-bit mixed scheme that preserves more of the model's distribution for probability-sensitive tasks. for RLHF or high-accuracy scoring we recommend q4_k_m; for cost-optimized throughput-oriented tasks int8 is fine. we'll mark recommended profiles per eval suite in the bundle.
[07:46] Jonas: do you ship eval harnesses for regression tests? we need to run our prompts to detect quality regressions after quantization or runtime changes.
[07:51] Miguel: yes, the artifacts include an eval harness, a sample prompt set, and a regression test script that outputs quality delta metrics. we include baseline outputs and thresholds.
[07:59] Ellen: on the security side we need to ensure private keys used for cosign never leave our HSM. can your install flow support HSM-based cosign verification?
[08:06] Miguel: yes, verification only needs the public key. for signing, obviously you'd sign with your HSM. our install scripts can be configured to use local HSM-provided keys for the final image promotion step — we documented that in the ops section.
[08:18] Samira: quick interrupt — wanted to make sure we're capturing next steps and owners. I'll summarize after Miguel finishes bench details. Miguel, continue on runtime perf caveats.
[08:28] Miguel: sure. two more caveats: cold-starts and batch packing. cold-starts hit p95 heavily; we recommend a short ‘keep-warm’ traffic generator in staging to keep KV caches warm for the most common routes. and batch packing — our runtime does continuous batching; if you allow large batch ceilings you'll get better throughput but higher single-request latency. tradeoff is tunable per route.
[08:50] Markus: is there a feature to pin routes to specific GPUs or capacity pools?
[08:53] Miguel: yes, routing policies in the on-prem control plane let you pin routes to pools, reserve capacity, and set fallback to smaller quantized variants on overload. that config is included in the runtime manifest.
[09:03] Aisha: in terms of lifecycle how do we do rollbacks if a patch breaks something in an air-gapped environment?
[09:08] Miguel: our delta bundles include prior-version artifacts so you can roll back to a known-good manifest. we recommend keeping at least two previous bundles on the offline registry. the installer has a --rollback-to flag.
[09:18] Jonas: can we automate canary traffic routing inside the air-gapped cluster?
[09:21] Miguel: yes, the runtime supports canary routes with traffic shifting policies. it’s all config-driven and works without egress.
[09:27] Ellen: about logging retention — can we control what logs leave the system when we eventually export for audits? we need a redact step.
[09:33] Miguel: logs are written locally and the export tool supports configurable redaction rules and a signed export package. we attach a manifest of what was redacted.
[09:40] Samira: ok we're ~50 minutes in. quick recap then action items.
[09:44] Samira: recap: we'll provide artifact tarball, checksums, driver manifest, offline license flow docs, bench runbook, and cosign verification scripts. Novus will confirm staging specs and allowed transfer method.
[09:56] Aisha: correct. Markus will gather staging hardware and kernel info. Ellen will send compliance list. Jonas will provision a small test cluster for the bench.
[10:03] Miguel: I'll produce the artifact bundle and the install/runbook and include the quantized model variants and eval harness. will attach sha256 for everything.
[10:10] Samira: any final questions?
[10:13] Ellen: one last: emergency patch SLA — do you have an SLA for delivering critical security fixes to air-gapped customers?
[10:19] Samira: yes, enterprise agreements include expedited offline transfers with a 72-hour target for high severity; we can detail that in the contract addendum.
[10:27] Aisha: sounds good. thanks everyone.
[10:30] Samira: thanks all, we'll follow up with the bundle and schedule the bench.
[10:35] End of recording.
